  3. If exports is not defined and the import has no file path, Node.js uses the entry point defined by main in package.json.

This resolution algorithm lets multiple versions of the same package coexist in one project — which happens frequently with indirect dependencies. Suppose your project depends on dep1 and dep2, but dep1 depends on lodash@3 while dep2 depends on lodash@4. Both can be satisfied by structuring node_modules like this:

Nested node_modules for conflicting versionstree
node_modules/
  dep1/
    node_modules/
      lodash/     # contains lodash@3
  dep2/
    node_modules/
      lodash/     # contains lodash@4

This works because import statements in dep1 and dep2 load lodash from their respective node_modules directories. Note that importing lodash in your own project’s index.mjs would fail to resolve.

Happily npm handles all this automatically, creating nested node_modules directories for indirect dependencies as needed. It also reduces duplication by hoisting indirect dependencies to the top level when there are no conflicting version requirements — so if dep1 and dep2 both depend on the same lodash version, the tree looks like this:

Hoisted, deduplicated treetree
node_modules/
  dep1/
  dep2/
  lodash/

Importing code from local packages

Import another module from your package with a relative path; import a dependency installed with npm by package name. But what if you want to import a module from another package on your system?

The standard solution is a symlink in node_modules so you can treat it as a dependency. npm offers two ways:

  • If you’re working on one of your project’s dependencies, run npm link <dependency-dir> to add a symlink to that package’s directory in node_modules.
  • If your project involves multiple interdependent packages, declare a workspaces list in package.json, which tells npm to create symlinks for all of those packages in node_modules when you run npm install. The packages can then import one another.

3.2.3 Syncing and updating dependencies

In npm’s early days developers faced a conundrum: checking the entire node_modules tree into version control created large diffs whenever a dependency changed, but the alternative risked inconsistencies whenever the project was installed elsewhere, because the dependency list in package.json didn’t contain enough information to reconstitute the same tree.

The solution was a lockfile, package-lock.json. When a user downloads a project and runs npm install, npm uses the lockfile to reconstitute the exact same node_modules tree. Today the norm is to commit package-lock.json but not node_modules, which keeps teams in sync with minimal effort. npm even has built-in merge conflict resolution for the lockfile: if you hit a conflict in package-lock.json, just run npm install.

Note JavaScript developers are divided on whether to use package-lock.json in packages consumed by others. Doing so freezes your package versions during development but doesn’t affect the downstream project, which can cause drift. As Sindre Sorhus put it: “If you use a lockfile for packages, your local dependency tree will not match the dependency tree of users having your package as a dependency.”

Having dependencies in both files confuses people: what’s the purpose of each? The key reason is that the lockfile rigidly specifies the exact version of every dependency in the tree, while package.json allows version ranges — which provide a smooth path for routine updates.

Take another look at the dependencies list in the http-server project:

package.json dependenciesJSON
"dependencies": {
  "express": "^5.1.0"
}

When we told npm to install express we only specified a major version. npm’s default behaviour is to find the latest exact version matching the specifier, then prefix the version in package.json with ^, creating a caret range.

To understand caret ranges you first need semver (“semantic versioning”). Each version has three components:

<major>.<minor>.<patch>

A version may also have a pre-release tag appended with a hyphen: 1.0.0-beta.1 is a pre-release considered earlier than 1.0.0.

The key to semver is the convention that incompatible changes must come with a newer major version number (pre-releases and versions below 1.0.0 are exceptions). As long as package authors honour that convention, newer minor and patch versions of the same dependency are safe to install.

That’s what the caret range means: it covers all newer but compatible versions, so you benefit from bug fixes and improvements. With "express": "^5.1.0", both express@5.1.1 and express@5.2.0 are compatible, but express@6.0.0 is not. (There’s a neat tool at semver.npmjs.com for trying out range specifiers and seeing which versions they cover.)

To update a package to the latest version within the range in package.json, use npm update --save <package>. The update command installs the new version in node_modules and revises the lockfile, while --save also modifies package.json to indicate the new version as the minimum.

To get the latest release regardless of the range, use npm install <package>@latest. Note that install saves its changes to package.json by default while update does not — which is why the --save flag is recommended when updating, so you keep a clear, readable record of all version changes.

3.2.4 Forking and patching dependencies

One great virtue of open source is that you’re free to change any dependency you use, fixing bugs or adding features without seeking the maintainers’ approval.

The traditional mechanism is to fork: create a full copy of the package’s repository, then apply your changes to the source. Most packages list their repository in package.json metadata, viewable with npm view <package> or by searching npmjs.com. Once you’ve forked, replace the version string in package.json with a direct git link to your fork:

Pointing at a forkJSON
"dependencies": {
  "express": "git+ssh://git@github.com:trevorburnham/express#5.1.0"  // #A
}
#A The # suffix indicates a git tag, which in this case points to a release version.

When you run npm install, npm downloads the repo, runs its build script (if defined) to generate the package artifacts, and adds them to node_modules as if it had downloaded the package from the registry.

Forking makes sense if you want to maintain a differentiated copy, but suppose you just want a quick bug fix while waiting for the maintainers to merge your pull request — or you need to change an indirect dependency. Editing code in node_modules directly isn’t stable: the change isn’t in version control, collaborators don’t receive it, and npm may overwrite it. The solution that persists patches is patch-package.

First install it as a dev dependency:

$ npm install --save-dev patch-package

The --save-dev flag adds the package to the devDependencies section instead of dependencies, differentiating what’s needed at runtime from what’s only needed in development. When you install a package, its transitive dependencies are installed but its transitive devDependencies are not.

Make your changes in node_modules, then run:

$ npx patch-package <package>

(The npx command runs binaries from packages — more in Section 3.3.2.) This generates a .patch file with your changes, which you can check into version control. To make sure the patch is applied every time npm installs that package, add a postinstall entry to the scripts section of package.json:

package.jsonJSON
"postinstall": "patch-package"

The postinstall script runs automatically after npm install and other commands that install packages into node_modules; lifecycle scripts are covered in section 3.3.1.

That’s dependency management, including changing dependencies via forking and patching. Next: how Node.js and npm can be used to write all kinds of scripts, from project automation to system management.

3.3 Scripting with Node.js

Once Node.js freed JavaScript from the confines of the browser, many developers discovered it was the only language they needed. They began using it for tasks that previously required a foray into shell scripting or firing up a Python or Ruby interpreter.

This section looks at several approaches to running scripts with Node.js, and at how to distribute scripts in an npm package anyone can run with a single command.

3.3.1 Defining scripts in package.json

The scripts section of package.json is a simple way to define short scripts:

package.jsonJSON
"scripts": {
  "hello": "echo 'Hello, scripts!'"
}

To execute a script, use npm run <script>:

$ npm run hello
Hello, scripts!

You can pass additional arguments, which get appended to the script. Use the -- separator before them so they aren’t treated as arguments to npm itself: 

$ npm run hello -- "And goodbye."
Hello, scripts! And goodbye.

A few script names have special rules:

  • The test, start, restart and stop scripts can be run with the shorthand npm <script> instead of npm run <script>.
  • If a script name starts with pre/post, it runs before/after the matching script. With prebuild, build and postbuild defined, npm run build runs all three in order.
  • Several npm commands trigger life cycle scripts: preinstall and postinstall run before and after npm install. Consult the npm documentation for details.
  • The prepare script runs automatically whenever the package is installed in another package — a common use case being compiling binaries.

One of the most powerful features is that npm puts every executable exported by the project’s installed packages on the PATH for scripts. A project with a dev dependency on ESLint might have:

package.jsonJSON
"scripts": {
  "lint": "eslint ."
}

Scripts can also use npm run to trigger other npm scripts:

package.jsonJSON
"scripts": {
  "lint": "eslint .",
  "build": "npm run lint && ./build.sh"
}

3.3.2 Writing executable scripts with Node.js

Node.js supports the shebang syntax (so called because the two characters #! are the “sharp” and “bang”), letting Mac/Linux systems treat a JavaScript file as an executable. Create hello.mjs:

hello.mjsES module
#!/usr/bin/env node
console.log("Hello, execution!");

Then chmod +x hello.mjs to give the file executable permissions. Now you can run it with ./hello.mjs instead of node hello.mjs.

However the script is run, Node.js resolves any import statements with the node_modules algorithm relative to the script’s location — so including dependencies is straightforward if the script ships as part of an npm package.

Node.js has several built-in APIs in its child_process namespace for calling arbitrary system commands, but they’re very verbose, requiring several parameters even for simple cases. Several npm packages therefore offer a more succinct syntax. One of the most popular is Google’s zx, which provides a function named $ that calls any shell command:

A script using zxES module
#!/usr/bin/env node
import { $ } from "zx";

const { stdout: dirContents } = await $`ls`;
console.log(
  dirContents.split("\n").includes("package.json")
    ? "Yes, this dir contains a package.json file."
    : "No, this dir does not contain a package.json file.",
);

Suppose you want to run a Node.js script where installing npm dependencies is impractical — a CI process with a firewall blocking the npm registry, for instance. In that case use a bundler such as esbuild to create a single JavaScript file containing the script and all its dependencies. Chapter 14 looks at esbuild more closely.

3.3.3 Running package executables with npx

Section 3.2.1 showed how npm packages provide entry points so import statements can reference their code once installed in node_modules. But packages aren’t limited to code: it’s common for them to distribute executables that can be run from the command line.

Typically such an executable is a JavaScript file written as described in Section 3.3.2. To make it an executable, add a bin entry to package.json:

package.jsonJSON
"bin": {
  "my-command": "bin/my-command.js"
}

When npm installs the package with that declaration, it creates an executable called my-command linked to the package’s bin/my-command.js. Once installed, the executable can be run from package.json scripts.

You can also run package executables directly with npx, a command bundled with npm. If ESLint is installed, npx runs its eslint executable without creating a scripts entry: 

$ npx eslint .

But npx’s power goes far beyond that. When you run npx <command> for a command that doesn’t match an executable in the local project, npx checks the registry for a package with that name. If it finds one, and if one of that package’s executables has the same name as the package (or it defines only one executable with any name), it temporarily installs the package and runs that executable.

Running a package executable straight from the registry is enormously convenient for packages you don’t need often, because it avoids the overhead of adding them to your node_modules tree and lockfile.

3.4 Summary

  1. Node.js is a popular JavaScript runtime that provides APIs for the file system, networking and other OS interactions.
  2. JavaScript code always runs in a single thread. Callbacks and promises allow I/O operations to be performed asynchronously, keeping the JavaScript thread unblocked.
  3. npm installs packages into a node_modules directory containing a project’s entire dependency tree, saves top-level dependencies in package.json, and uses package-lock.json to track the full contents of node_modules for version control.
  4. Bare specifiers — imports using a package name rather than a complete file path — are resolved by recursing through the closest node_modules directory.
  5. Node.js supports executable scripts with the shebang syntax, and packages can make executables available by declaring them in the bin field of package.json.
  6. npx runs executables from other packages; if the specified package isn’t installed, it’s downloaded from the registry and temporarily installed while the command runs.

Source

Chapter 3, “Working with Node.js and npm”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 44–60 of the PDF edition in this repository.

Listing 3.1 is reproduced in full, together with the command output and short snippets that accompany it; the book’s #A–#D callouts are kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet. Chapter 3 contains no figures — the stopwatch icon used for the “don’t block the thread” note is the book’s performance-tip icon, embedded in Chapter 1.

Chapter 4

Building web applications

This chapter covers

  • Steps in the lifecycle of a web application
  • How HTML and the DOM are related
  • The order of JavaScript code execution
  • Writing interactive HTML with JSX

JavaScript began as a language for adding interactivity to websites. At first it was an enhancement, modifying the HTML and CSS on the page to add luxuries like animations and form validation. But over time JavaScript became essential: today it’s common for websites to be built with nothing but JavaScript, with developers thinking in terms of components instead of HTML tags and CSS rules.

That abstraction made it easier than ever to build complex web experiences — but losing sight of the browser’s underlying workings comes at a cost: a JavaScript-heavy website can easily degrade into a miserably slow experience.

This chapter explores the lifecycle of client-side web applications, end to end:

  • How HTML is used to build the DOM, a representation of the page’s content.
  • How JavaScript interacts with the page, and how the event loop lets code respond to users.
  • How modern frameworks like React hybridise JavaScript and HTML with a language called JSX.

4.1 The lifecycle overview

The lifecycle of a typical client-side web application begins with the user typing a URL into the browser’s address bar or clicking a link. Say we want to look up a term and go to Google’s homepage: we type google.com, as shown in Figure 4.1.

On behalf of the user, the browser formulates a request that is sent to a server (#2), which processes the request (#3) and formulates a response usually composed of HTML, CSS and JavaScript code. The moment the browser receives this response (#4) is when our client-side web application truly starts coming to life.

Because client-side web applications are Graphical User Interface (GUI) applications, their lifecycle follows similar phases to other GUI applications (think desktop or mobile apps) and is carried out in two steps:

  1. Page building — set up the user interface.
  2. Event handling — enter a loop (#5) waiting for events to occur (#6), and start invoking event handlers.

The lifecycle ends when the user closes or leaves the web page (#7).

Now let’s look at an example application with a simple UI that reacts to user actions: every time a user presses a key, a message is displayed. We’ll use it throughout the chapter.

Listing 4.1 — Small web application with a GUI reacting to eventsHTML
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Web App Lifecycle</title>
  <style>
    #event-list li {
      font: 1.25rem system-ui;
      padding: 0.25rem 0;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <ul id="event-list"></ul>
  <script>
    const eventList = document.querySelector("#event-list");

    const appendToEventList = (message) => {                // #A
      const messageElement = document.createElement("li"); // #A
      messageElement.textContent = message;                // #A
      eventList.appendChild(messageElement);               // #A
    };                                                     // #A

    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {  // #B
      appendToEventList('Event "DOMContentLoaded" fired'); // #B
    });                                                    // #B

    document.addEventListener("keydown", (evt) => {      // #C
      appendToEventList(                                 // #C
        `Event "keydown" fired with key = "${evt.key}"`  // #C
      );                                                 // #C
    });                                                  // #C

    appendToEventList("End of script reached");
  </script>
</body>
</html>
#A Defines a function that adds a message to the event list on the page
#B Attaches a DOMContentLoaded event handler to the document
#C Attaches a keydown event handler to the document

The key elements in Listing 4.1 are:

  1. A <style> tag with a CSS rule intended to make the event list more readable.
  2. The event list element, a <ul> (unordered list).
  3. A <script> tag with our JavaScript code.

Our script defines an appendToEventList function that, when invoked, appends a new list item element to the event list element. The first event type we listen for is DOMContentLoaded, which fires when the browser has finished parsing the entire HTML document. The second is keydown, which fires when a key on the keyboard is pressed. Lastly, we append a message to the event list at the end of our JavaScript code.

If you open this HTML document in a browser and then type “asdf,” you should see this output:

file:///…/index.html
  • End of script reached
  • Event "DOMContentLoaded" fired
  • Event "keydown" fired with key = "a"
  • Event "keydown" fired with key = "s"
  • Event "keydown" fired with key = "d"
  • Event "keydown" fired with key = "f"

We’ll use this example application to explore and illustrate the differences between the phases of the web application lifecycle. Let’s start with the page-building phase.

4.2 The page-building phase

Before a web application can be interacted with or even displayed, the page must be built from the information in the HTML document received from the server. To do that, the browser parses the HTML and builds the Document Object Model (DOM), a tree representing the contents of the page.

When the parser encounters a <script> tag, the browser’s default behaviour is to stop parsing the document and execute the script before continuing. (That default can be overridden by attributes on the <script> tag such as async, defer and module — see MDN on the script element.) When a script runs, it can access and modify the DOM tree.

4.2.1 Parsing HTML and building the DOM

The page-building phase starts with the browser receiving the HTML code, which is used as a base on top of which the browser builds the page’s UI. It does this by parsing the HTML one element at a time; every HTML element is represented as a node in the DOM. Figure 4.3 shows the DOM of the example page built up to the point where the first script element is reached.

Notice how the nodes are organised so that every node except the first (the root html node, #1) has exactly one parent. For example, the head node (#2) has the html node (#1) as its parent. At the same time a node can have any number of children: the html node (#1) has two children, the head node (#2) and the body node (#7). Children of the same element are siblings.

It’s important to emphasise that although HTML and the DOM are closely linked, they aren’t one and the same. Think of the HTML code as a blueprint the browser follows when constructing the initial DOM — the UI — of the page. The browser can even fix problems it finds in that blueprint in order to create a valid DOM. Consider Figure 4.4.

Figure 4.4 shows erroneous HTML in which a paragraph element is placed in the head element. The head is intended to provide general page information — title, character encodings, external styles and scripts — not to define page content. Because this is an error, the browser silently fixes it by constructing the correct DOM (at right), in which the paragraph is placed in the body, where page content belongs.

The HTML and DOM specifications

HTML and DOM both have living standards, at html.spec.whatwg.org and dom.spec.whatwg.org.

Why separate standards? The DOM standard is “platform neutral” — it isn’t tied specifically to HTML. In fact, the vector graphics format SVG also uses the DOM standard.

As a JavaScript Ninja you’ll rarely need these specs; the MDN docs on HTML and the DOM are more enlightening.

4.2.2 Executing JavaScript code

When the browser encounters a synchronous script node during the page-building phase, it pauses DOM construction and starts executing the global JavaScript code contained in the script element instead. Let’s walk through the example from Listing 4.1.

First we call querySelector on the global document object — which represents the page’s DOM tree — to get the element with the ID event-list:

Getting the list elementJavaScript
const eventList = document.querySelector("#event-list");

Then we define a function called appendToEventList:

Defining the helperJavaScript
const appendToEventList = (message) => {
  const messageElement = document.createElement("li");
  messageElement.textContent = message;
  eventList.appendChild(messageElement);
};

After that we attach some event listeners to the document (section 4.3). Lastly we make a single call to appendToEventList, causing an li element to be created and added as the first child of the event-list element:

The call at the end of the scriptJavaScript
appendToEventList("End of script reached");

Figure 4.5 shows the state of the DOM after the script has been executed, but before any events have fired.

Here the JavaScript code modifies the current DOM by creating a new element and inserting it. In general JavaScript can modify the DOM to any degree: creating new nodes and modifying or removing existing ones. Section 4.4 looks at the now-common practice of using JavaScript compiled from a templating language to create entire pages from scratch.

Once the JavaScript engine executes the last line of code in the script element, the browser exits JavaScript execution mode and continues building DOM nodes from the remaining HTML. It’s important to note that the application’s global state persists in the meantime: user-defined global variables created while one script element ran are normally accessible to code in other script elements, because the global window object that stores them is alive for the entire lifecycle of the page.

Finally, when the browser runs out of HTML elements to process, the page-building phase is complete and the second part of the lifecycle begins: event handling.

4.3 Event handling

Client-side web applications are GUI applications, which means they react to different kinds of events: mouse moves, clicks, key presses and so on. For that reason, the JavaScript executed during the page-building phase can — besides influencing global state and modifying the DOM — register event listeners (also known as handlers): functions the browser executes when an event occurs. With handlers we provide interactivity. But before looking at registration, let’s cover the general ideas.

4.3.1 Event-handling overview

The browser execution environment is at its core based on the idea that only a single piece of code can execute at once: the single-threaded execution model. Think of a line at the bank. Everyone gets into a single line and waits their turn to be “processed” by the tellers — but with JavaScript, only one teller window is open! Customers (events) are processed one at a time as their turn comes. All it takes is one person who thinks it’s appropriate to do their financial planning for the entire fiscal year while at the window to gum up the works.

Whenever an event occurs the browser should execute the associated handler. But there’s no guarantee of extremely patient users who always wait an appropriate amount of time before triggering another event. So the browser needs a way to keep track of events that have occurred but not yet been processed. It uses an event queue, as shown in Figure 4.6.

All events are placed in the same queue, in the order the browser detects them. As shown in the middle of Figure 4.6, the event-handling process can then be described with a simple flowchart:

  • The browser checks the head of the event queue.
  • If there are no events, the browser keeps checking.
  • If there is an event at the head, the browser takes it and executes the associated handler (if one exists). During that execution the rest of the events patiently wait in the queue for their turn.

Because only one event is handled at a time, we have to be extra careful about how long handlers take: writing slow handlers leads to unresponsive web applications! (Chapter 8 returns to the event loop and shows exactly how it affects perceived performance.)

Note that the browser mechanism that puts events onto the queue is external to the page-building and event-handling phases. The work of determining that an event occurred and pushing it onto the queue doesn’t participate in the thread handling events. You may have experienced this yourself: you click a button on a page that has frozen because of some expensive JavaScript or a layout calculation; frustrated, you click it again and again — and when the page starts working, it responds to all three clicks!

Events are asynchronous

Events can occur at unpredictable times and in an unpredictable order (it’s tricky to force users to press keys or click in a particular order). So the handling of events — and therefore the invocation of their handling functions — is asynchronous.

Among others, these types of events can occur:

  • Browser events, such as when a page finishes loading or is unloaded
  • Network events, such as the response to a fetch request
  • User events, such as mouse clicks, mouse moves and key presses
  • Timer events, such as when a timeout expires or a promise resolves

Event handling is central to web applications, and you’ll see it again and again in this book. In a typical web application, the vast majority of the JavaScript that runs runs in response to events.

4.3.2 Registering event handlers

Event handlers are functions we want executed whenever a particular event occurs. To make that happen we must notify the browser that we’re interested in the event: event-handler registration.

In modern web applications events are typically registered with the addEventListener method on a DOM element. Consider this excerpt from the script in Listing 4.1:

Listing 4.2 — Registering event handlersJavaScript
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {  // #A
  appendToEventList('Event "DOMContentLoaded" fired'); // #A
});                                                    // #A

document.addEventListener("keydown", (evt) => {                       // #B
  appendToEventList(`Event "keydown" fired with key = "${evt.key}"`); // #B
});                                                                   // #B
#A Registers a handler for the DOMContentLoaded event
#B Registers a handler for the keydown event

An interesting feature of DOM events is that they can be intercepted on a different node than the one that fired them. DOMContentLoaded fires directly from the document node, so there we handle the event at its source. But keydown fires from wherever the keyboard focus is — and yet, even if we add an <input> to the page and type in it, the handler attached to document still fires. That’s thanks to a DOM feature known as bubbling, discussed along with its close cousin event capturing in Chapter 16.

4.4 Writing interactive HTML with JSX

So far all of our page content has been written either directly as HTML or by using the DOM API. Starting in the mid-2010s, web developers began embracing a more abstract approach: the React library introduced JSX, a language that mashes JavaScript and HTML together.

At first glance JSX looks just like JavaScript — but it lets you use HTML syntax to define values:

A value written in JSXJSX
const link = <a href="https://manning.com">Manning</a>;

JSX ultimately compiles to JavaScript, with HTML tags converted to objects. The exact conversion depends on the JSX compiler and its settings, but the example above would compile to something like this:

The compiled formJavaScript
const link = _jsx("a", {
  href: "https://manning.com",
  children: "Manning"
});

That _jsx function comes from the runtime library in use. React is the original JSX runtime and remains the most popular, but several other libraries support JSX too. The rest of the code is a straightforward object representation of the HTML.

Listing 4.3 reimplements this chapter’s example in React using JSX (you can run it at reactplayground.vercel.app). To keep the example simple, the keydown handler is attached to an <input> element rather than the document. Document-level listeners are possible in React, but require an extra hook called useEffect.

Listing 4.3 — An event list component in ReactJSX
import React, { useState } from "react";

export default function EventList() {                       // #A
  const [events, setEvents] = useState(["Initial event"]);  // #B

  return (
    <ul id="event-list">
      {events.map((str) => (                        // #C
        <li>{str}</li>                          // #C
      ))}                                            // #C
      <li>
        <input                                    // #D
          onKeyDown={(evt) => {                    // #D
            setEvents(                             // #D
              events.concat(`Event "keydown" fired with key =
                "${evt.key}"`),                        // #D
            );                                       // #D
          }}                                         // #D
        />                                          // #D
      </li>
    </ul>
  );
}
#A Defines a React component named EventList
#B Defines a list of event descriptions as state for the component
#C Adds a list item to the DOM for every event description
#D Renders an <input> with a keydown handler that adds to the list of event descriptions

The magic of this JSX is that all the DOM interaction is abstracted away: there’s no createElement, no appendChild, no addEventListener. React takes care of all of it. Instead we think about our application in terms of its state: any modification to the events array — adding, removing or changing items — results in React updating the DOM to match the tree of elements returned from our component.

React provides that simple, elegant developer experience by being quite sophisticated under the hood. It uses the tree of elements from all the React components on the page to construct a virtual DOM, its own internal representation of what the page’s DOM should be. Then it performs reconciliation: comparing the current virtual DOM to its previous version and altering the page’s DOM according to the diff.

This approach has become the dominant paradigm in web development, but it has come at a cost. If content is served as HTML, the user sees the page as soon as that HTML is parsed; if the page is defined in JavaScript, the browser must finish running that code first. That tends to be much slower, for several reasons:

  • The JavaScript representation of a DOM node is generally larger and more expensive to parse than the equivalent HTML tag.
  • The framework itself adds a substantial amount of code that must execute before the compiled JSX can.
  • Depending on how the bundle was built, it may include code for parts of the page the user can’t see yet, or even for other pages.

As a JavaScript Ninja it’s important to use frameworks responsibly: consider lighter-weight frameworks such as Solid; split your bundles so code not needed for the initial render doesn’t run until later; and, if possible, use server-side rendering (SSR), which lets the browser get the full page before running any JavaScript.

4.5 Summary

  1. The HTML code received by the browser is used as a blueprint for creating the DOM, an internal representation of the structure of a client-side web application.
  2. JavaScript code can read and modify the DOM, adding interactivity to web applications.
  3. DOM events can be enqueued at any time, but their handlers won’t run until the JavaScript thread is free.
  4. JSX abstracts away the process of updating the DOM, allowing web applications to be written as a set of reusable components that render DOM trees based on their state.

Source

Chapter 4, “Building web applications”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 61–76 of the PDF edition in this repository.

All six of the chapter’s figures (4.1–4.6) and all three listings (4.1–4.3) are included above, embedded as data URIs with the book’s captions; the #A–#D callouts are kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet.

Chapter 5

First-class functions for the novice: definitions and arguments

This chapter covers

  • The ways to define a function
  • What makes JavaScript functions so powerful
  • How TypeScript can catch bad function calls before they happen

Turning to this part of the book on JavaScript fundamentals, you might be surprised that the first topic is functions rather than objects. Objects get plenty of attention in part 3 — but when it comes down to brass tacks, the main difference between writing JavaScript like the average Jill (or Joe) and writing it like a JavaScript ninja is understanding JavaScript as a functional language. The sophistication of every line of JavaScript you ever write hinges on that realisation.

This isn’t a book for rank beginners: it assumes you know enough object fundamentals to get by (chapter 9 goes deeper). But really understanding functions is the single most important weapon you can wield — so important that this and the following three chapters are devoted to it.

Most important: in JavaScript, functions are first-class objects, or first-class citizens. They coexist with — and can be treated like — any other object. Just like more mundane data types they can be referenced by variables, declared with literals, and even passed as parameters. This chapter tours the ways of declaring functions, then exploits functions as first-class objects, and finally looks at parameters versus arguments, rest parameters and default parameters.

Do you know?

  • What’s the difference between an arrow function and a function expression?
  • How can you write a function that caches its return value?
  • When might you want to use default parameter values in a function?

5.1 Defining functions

JavaScript provides a bevy of ways to define functions:

FormWhat it looks like, and what’s notable
Function declaration The most traditional syntax, familiar from any C-derived language: the function keyword, a name, a parameter list and a body. Unique in that the function can be called before it’s defined (chapter 6).
Function expression The function keyword used inside another statement, such as a variable declaration or assignment. Unlike a declaration, it doesn’t require a name.
Arrow function ES2015 added the => syntax between the parameter list and the body. More succinct, and unique in how it handles this.
Method definition A function as a property of an object literal or class, using syntax like a declaration minus the function keyword. Behaves like a function expression; works with get/set (chapter 10).
Class field ES2022 syntax for defining functions as class fields — succinct, with some unique features (chapter 9).
Function constructor Build a function dynamically by passing strings for its arguments and body to Function. Rarely used, and to be treated with the same caution as eval.
All six forms, side by sideJavaScript
function myFun() { return 1; }             // declaration
const myFun = function(a) { return a; }     // expression
const myFun = (a, b) => a * b;                 // arrow
const myObj = { myFun(key) { return this[key]; }}  // method
class MyClass { myFun = () => this.x * this.y; }      // class field
new Function('a', 'b', 'return a + b');          // constructor

There are also generators, a special type of function considered separately in chapter 8 — any function definition containing a * character is one. This chapter explores the behavioural differences between declarations, expressions and arrow functions; the book returns to them repeatedly.

5.1.1 Function declarations and function expressions

A function declared with the function keyword and a name is a function declaration (figure 5.1).

Every function declaration starts with a mandatory function keyword, followed by a mandatory name and a list of optional comma-separated parameter names inside mandatory parentheses. The body — a potentially empty list of statements — must be enclosed in braces. One important restriction affects where you can put a declaration: it must be its own statement, not a mere expression. Listing 5.1 demonstrates a couple of declarations:

Listing 5.1 — Examples of function declarationsJavaScript
function samurai() {              // #A
  return "samurai here";       // #A
}                                // #A

function ninja() {                // #B
  function hiddenNinja() {      // #C
    return "ninja here";        // #C
  }                              // #C
  return hiddenNinja();
}
#A Defines function samurai in the global code
#B Defines function ninja in the global code
#C Defines function hiddenNinja within the ninja function

A function defined within another function is perfectly normal in JavaScript — included here to emphasise how important functions are.

Note Functions contained in other functions raise tricky questions about scope and identifier resolution. Save them for chapter 7, which revisits this case in detail.

Since functions are first-class objects they can be created via literals, assigned to variables and properties, and used as arguments and return values. Because they’re such fundamental constructs, JavaScript lets us treat them as any other expression — just as we can use number literals:

Expressions, for comparisonJavaScript
let a = 3;
myFunction(4);

…so too can we use functions in the same locations:

Functions in expression positionJavaScript
let a = function() {};
myFunction(function(){});

Functions that are always part of another statement — the right side of an assignment, or an argument to another function — are function expressions. They’re great because they let us define functions exactly where we need them, making code easier to understand. Listing 5.2 shows the differences.

Listing 5.2 — Function declarations and function expressionsJavaScript
function myFunctionDeclaration(){        // #A
  function innerFunction() {}           // #B
}

const myFunc = function(){};            // #C

myFunc(function(){                       // #D
  return function(){};                // #E
});

(function namedFunctionExpression () {       // #F
})();                                    // #F

+function(){}();      // #G
-function(){}();      // #G
!function(){}();      // #G
~function(){}();      // #G
#A Standalone function declaration
#B Inner function declaration
#C Function expression as part of a variable declaration assignment
#D Function expression as an argument of a function call
#E Function expression as a function return value
#F Named function expression as part of a function call that will be immediately invoked
#G Function expressions that will be immediately invoked, as arguments to unary operators

Besides position in code, there’s one more difference: for declarations the name is mandatory, whereas for expressions it’s completely optional. Declarations must be named because the name is the only way to invoke them — and a function that can’t be invoked would be no function at all! Expressions are parts of other expressions, so there are other ways to invoke them: assign one to a variable and use the variable, const doNothing = function(){}; doNothing();, or pass one as an argument and invoke it through the matching parameter:

Invoking a function expression via a parameterJavaScript
function doSomething(action) {
  action();
}

Immediate functions

Function expressions can be placed in positions that look odd at first — such as where we’d normally expect a function identifier. Take a closer look at that construct (figure 5.2).

To make a function call we use an expression that evaluates to a function, followed by a pair of call parentheses that may contain arguments. In the most basic call, that expression is an identifier (left). But it needn’t be a simple identifier — it can be any expression that evaluates to a function, and a function expression is a simple way to write one. On the right we create a function and then immediately invoke that newly created function: an immediately invoked function expression (IIFE), or immediate function for short.

Parentheses around function expressions

Why the parentheses around the expression? Purely syntactical: the parser must differentiate declarations from expressions.

Leave them out, with the call as a separate statement function(){}(3), and you get a parser error — any statement starting with function must be a declaration, and a declaration must have a name. Using a named function fails differently: because a declaration is a complete statement, function f(){}(3) parses as two statements, a declaration and the number 3 by itself — a no-op.

Wrapping the function in parentheses makes the parser treat it as an expression, so (3) becomes a call. Alternatively, wrap both the function and the call: (function(){}(3)) — inside parentheses, function unambiguously creates an expression.

The last four expressions in listing 5.2 are variations of the same theme, often found in JavaScript libraries. Instead of parentheses, unary operators — +, -, ! and ~ — signal to the engine that it’s dealing with an expression rather than a statement. The results aren’t stored anywhere, so computationally only the calls matter.

5.1.2 Arrow functions

Because we use so many functions in JavaScript, some syntactic sugar for creating them more succinctly makes developers’ lives more pleasant. Consider this example:

Function expressionJavaScript
const hypotenuse = function(a, b) {
  return Math.sqrt(a ** 2 + b ** 2);
};

Now the same function with arrow syntax:

Arrow functionJavaScript
const hypotenuse = (a, b) => Math.sqrt(a ** 2 + b ** 2);

Much more succinct: no clutter from the function keyword, and both the braces and the return keyword can be omitted. The new operator =>, an equals sign followed by a greater-than sign, is used only for arrow functions, so its official ECMAScript name is the arrow function operator.

The arrow syntax offers a few variations, starting with the simplest form — one parameter, returning an expression:

The simplest arrow formJavaScript
param => expression

Used in the following listing, which also introduces console.assert:

Listing 5.3 — Comparing an arrow function and a function expressionJavaScript
const greet = name => "Greetings " + name;   // #A

console.assert(greet("Oishi") === "Greetings Oishi",
  "Oishi is properly greeted");

const anotherGreet = function(name){    // #B
  return "Greetings " + name;            // #B
};                                       // #B

console.assert(anotherGreet("Oishi") === "Greetings Oishi",
  "Again, Oishi is properly greeted");
#A Defines an arrow function
#B Defines an equivalent function expression

Making assertions with console.assert

Consider this example:

console.assert("hello assert" === ["hello", "assert"].join(""),
  "joined strings are separated with a space")

The first argument is an expression whose premise is asserted. If it’s “truthy” (see Appendix A) the assertion passes; otherwise it fails. The second argument is the message emitted on failure, and by convention describes what we expect to happen.

Running this example produces:

Assertion failed: joined strings are separated with a space

Change join("") to join(" ") and there’s no output, because the assertion passes. No news is good news when it comes to assertions.

In general an arrow function can be defined in two ways, as figure 5.3 shows.

The definition starts with an optional comma-separated parameter list. With no parameters or more than one, the list must be in parentheses; with exactly one, the parentheses are optional. Then comes the mandatory fat-arrow operator, telling us and the engine that this is an arrow function.

After the arrow there are two options. For a simple function, put an expression there and the function’s return value is that expression’s value — as in const greet = name => "Greetings " + name;, whose return value concatenates "Greetings " with the name parameter. For anything more involved, include a block of code:

An arrow function with a blockJavaScript
const greet = name => {
  const helloString = "Greetings ";
  return helloString + name;
};

In that case the return value behaves as in a standard function: undefined without a return statement, the value of the return expression with one.

So far these are syntactic differences. There’s also an important behavioural difference when this is used in the body — the subject of the next chapter on function contexts.

5.2 The versatility of JavaScript functions

In JavaScript, objects enjoy certain capabilities. They can be assigned to variables, array entries and properties:

Objects: assignmentJavaScript
const ninja = {};      // #A
ninjaArray.push({});   // #B
ninja.data = {};       // #C
#A Assigns a new object to a variable
#B Adds a new object to an array
#C Assigns a new object as a property of another object

They can be passed as arguments to functions:

Objects: argumentsJavaScript
function hide(ninja){
  ninja.visibility = false;
}
hide({});     // #A
#A A newly created object passed as an argument to a function

They can be returned as values from functions:

Objects: return valuesJavaScript
function returnNewNinja() {
  return {};     // #A
}
#A Returns a new object from a function

And they can possess properties that are dynamically created and assigned:

Objects: dynamic propertiesJavaScript
const ninja = {};
ninja.name = "Hanzo";   // #A
#A Creates a new property on an object

It turns out that in JavaScript — unlike many other programming languages — we can do almost the exact same things with functions.

5.2.1 Functions as first-class objects

Functions possess all the capabilities of objects and are thus treated like any other object in the language. We say they’re first-class objects, which can also be:

  • Assigned to variables, array entries and properties of other objects
  • Passed as arguments to other functions
  • Returned from other functions
Functions: assignmentJavaScript
const ninjaFunction = function() {};   // #A
ninjaArray.push(function() {});          // #B
ninja.data = function() {};               // #C
#A Assigns a new function to a variable
#B Adds a new function to an array
#C Assigns a new function as a property of another object
Functions: argumentsJavaScript
function call(ninjaFunction){
  ninjaFunction();
}
call(function() {});   // #A
#A A newly created function passed as an argument to a function
Functions: return valuesJavaScript
function returnNewNinjaFunction() {
  return function(){};   // #A
}
#A Returns a new function
Functions: dynamic propertiesJavaScript
let ninjaFunction = function() {};
ninjaFunction.ninja = "Hanzo";   // #A
#A Adds a new property to a function

Whatever we can do with objects, we can do with functions. Functions are objects, just with an additional, special capability of being invokable: they can be called in order to perform an action.

Functional programming in JavaScript

Having functions as first-class objects is the first step toward functional programming, a style focused on solving problems by composing functions instead of specifying sequences of steps as in imperative programming. It can help write code that’s easier to test, extend and modularise.

But it’s a big topic, and this book only nods at it (chapter 11, for instance). For more, see Functional Programming in JavaScript by Luis Atencio (Manning, 2016).

5.2.2 Callback functions

Whenever we set up a function to be called at a later time — by the browser during the event-handling phase, or by other code — we’re setting up a callback. The term stems from establishing a function that other code will later “call back” at an appropriate point of execution.

Callbacks are essential to using JavaScript effectively, and you almost certainly already use them — for button clicks, receiving server data, or animating UI. Before the complex real-world cases, let’s strip the concept bare with a completely useless function that takes a reference to another function and calls it:

The useless functionJavaScript
function useless(ninjaCallback) {
  return ninjaCallback();
}

Useless as it is, it demonstrates passing a function as an argument and invoking it through the passed parameter. We can test it with listing 5.4.

Listing 5.4 — A simple callback exampleJavaScript
const text = "Domo arigato!";

console.log("Before defining functions");

function useless(ninjaCallback) {          // #A
  console.log ("In useless function");      // #A
  return ninjaCallback();              // #A
}                                      // #A

function getText() {                     // #B
  console.log ("In getText function");    // #B
  return text;                       // #B
}                                    // #B

console.log("Before making all the calls");

console.assert(useless(getText) === text,       // #C
  "The useless function works! " + text);  // #C

console.log("After the calls have been made");
#A Defines a function that takes a callback function and immediately invokes it
#B Defines a simple function that returns a global variable
#C Calls our useless function with the getText function as a callback

The console.log calls let us track execution. Running this produces:

Before defining functions
Before making all the calls
In useless function
In getText function
After the calls have been made

As figure 5.4 shows, we pass getText into useless as an argument, so inside the body of useless it can be referenced through the callback parameter. The ninjaCallback() call then executes getText: the function passed as an argument is called back by useless.

This is easy because JavaScript’s functional nature lets us deal with functions as first-class objects. We can even take it a step further and define the callback inline:

Callback defined inlineJavaScript
const text = "Domo arigato!";

function useless(ninjaCallback) {
  return ninjaCallback();
}

console.assert(useless(function () { return text;}) === text,  // #A
  "The useless function works! " + text);
#A Defines a callback function directly as an argument

One of JavaScript’s most important features is the ability to create functions anywhere an expression can appear. Beyond making code compact and easy to understand (definitions near where they’re used), this eliminates the need to pollute the namespace with names for functions referenced only once.

Callbacks can also be called in response to events — think back to chapter 3’s example:

An event handler is a callbackJavaScript
document.body.addEventListener("mousemove", function() {
  const second = document.getElementById("second");
  addMessage(second, "Event: mousemove");
});

That’s a callback too, defined as an event handler for mousemove and called by the browser when the event occurs.

Sorting with a comparator

Almost as soon as we have a collection of data we’ll need to sort it. Say we have an array of numbers in a random order — 0, 3, 2, 5, 7, 4, 8, 1. That might be fine, but sooner or later we’ll want to rearrange it.

Implementing sorting algorithms isn’t trivial: choose the best algorithm, implement it, adapt it to the current need, and avoid introducing bugs. Of those tasks only the sorting order is application-specific. Luckily all JavaScript arrays have sort, which asks only that we define a comparison algorithm telling it how values should be ordered.

This is where callbacks jump in. Instead of letting the algorithm decide what goes before what, we provide a function that performs the comparison; the algorithm calls it whenever it needs one. The callback should return a positive number if the order of the passed values should be reversed, a negative number if not, and zero if the values are equal. Subtracting the values produces exactly that:

Sorting with a callback comparatorJavaScript
const values = [0, 3, 2, 5, 7, 4, 8, 1];
values.sort((value1, value2) => value1 - value2);

No need to think about the low-level details of the algorithm — that’s up to the runtime. All sort needs is a function to call every time it compares two items. The functional approach lets us create a function as a standalone entity, pass it as an argument, and have it accepted as a parameter, just like any other object type. That’s first-class status in play.

Note You can use sort without a comparator, but it may not do what you expect: the default converts each value to a string and compares alphabetically, so 10 comes before 2! Even for string arrays the default isn’t ideal, because it was written with only ASCII in mind. To sort strings in the order users expect, use localeCompare.

5.3 Fun with functions

This section examines ways to take advantage of functions’ versatility:

  • Storing functions in a collection makes related functions easy to manage — callbacks that must fire when something of interest occurs.
  • Attaching metadata makes functions easier to debug, even with minified code.
  • Memoization caches a function’s previous results, improving the performance of later invocations.

5.3.1 Storing functions in a collection

Sometimes we need collections of unique functions — for instance, the callbacks to invoke when an event occurs. The challenge is determining which functions are new and which are already resident; duplicates are undesirable, since a single event would then call the same callback multiple times.

The obvious but naïve approach is to keep an array and loop through it checking for duplicates. That performs poorly, and as a ninja we want things to work well, not merely work. Fortunately, since functions are objects, we can store them in a Set — a built-in collection that guarantees uniqueness. Adding an object that’s already in the set does nothing:

Listing 5.5 — Storing a collection of unique functionsJavaScript
let count = 0;
const increment = () => {
  count++;
};

const funcSet = new Set();  // #A
funcSet.add(increment);     // #B
funcSet.add(increment);     // #B

funcSet.forEach((func) => func());                // #C
console.assert(count === 1,                       // #D
  "The function was only added to the set once"); // #D
#A Creates an empty set
#B Adds the function to the set, but only if it isn’t already in the set
#C Calls each function in the set once
#D Confirms that increment is only called once

“Uniqueness” here means reference equality: the second funcSet.add(increment) has no effect because the function referenced by increment is already in the set. Nothing stops us from declaring two functions with the same body and adding both:

Same body, different referencesJavaScript
funcSet.add(() => { count++; }); // Adds a function to the set
funcSet.add(() => { count++; }); // Adds another function to the set

5.3.2 Attaching metadata to functions

Since functions are objects, we can attach arbitrary data to them:

Data on a functionJavaScript
function func() {}
func.str = "a string";

console.assert(func.str === "a string",
  "We can attach data to functions");

But just because we can doesn’t mean we should. Sticking data to a function feels sloppy, mainly because of encapsulation: attaching data lets all code with access to the function read and write it. If only the declaring module needs the data, a separate variable in that module’s scope is more elegant.

Modern frameworks do use the feature for one purpose: metadata describing the function. In React you can attach a displayName to a component function to see its name while debugging with React DevTools:

Listing 5.6 — Attaching a displayName to a React component functionJSX
function HelloWorld() {              // #A
  return <p>Hello, React world!</p>    // #B
}

HelloWorld.displayName = "HelloWorld";
#A In React, capitalising a function name indicates that it’s a “component” that renders HTML
#B This is JSX code, an extension of JavaScript that allows HTML to be mixed in

Note You can read the name a function was declared with via its name property — that’s where stack-trace names come from. So why attach a displayName with the same value? Mainly because function names are usually lost when code is minified, whereas attached properties like displayName are preserved.

By attaching metadata directly to the function, all code that consumes it can also access that metadata.

5.3.3 Memoizing functions

Memoization (no, that’s not a typo) is building a function capable of remembering its previously computed values. Whenever the function computes a result we store it alongside the arguments, so a later invocation with the same arguments returns the stored result instead of recomputing. That can markedly increase performance by avoiding needless complex computation. Memoization is particularly useful for animation calculations, searching data that doesn’t change often, or any time-consuming maths.

As an example, here is a simplistic (and not especially efficient) algorithm for computing prime numbers — a stand-in for the expensive computations (MD5 hashing, say) where the technique really pays off:

Listing 5.7 — Computing a prime numberJavaScript
const isPrime = (value) => {
  if (value === 0 || value === 1) {        // #A
    return false; // 0 and 1 are not prime // #A
  }                                        // #A
  for (let i = 2; i < value; i++) {      // #B
    if (value % i === 0) {              // #B
      return false;                        // #B
    }                                      // #B
  }                                        // #B
  return true;                            // #C
};

console.assert(isPrime(5), "5 is prime!");
#A Handles 0 and 1 as special cases
#B Returns false if any previous integer is a divisor
#C Returns true because no divisors were found

Imagine this function is called repeatedly with the same value. An easy optimisation is to memoize it, caching the answer for each value — in JavaScript, with a wrapper function:

Listing 5.8 — Memoizing a functionJavaScript
function memoize(func) {                 // #A
  const cache = new Map();             // #B
  return (arg) => {                       // #C
    if (!cache.has(arg)) {            // #C
      cache.set(arg, func(arg));          // #C
    }                                    // #C
    return cache.get(arg);              // #C
  };                                     // #C
}

const memoizedIsPrime = memoize(isPrime);            // #D
console.assert(memoizedIsPrime (5), "5 is prime!");  // #D
#A Defines a function called memoize that takes another function as an argument
#B When memoize is called, it defines a map to use as a cache
#C The return value of memoize is a new function that caches the result of calling func
#D The memoized version of isPrime works as a drop-in replacement with built-in caching

The caching logic could live inside isPrime, but the wrapper provides elegant encapsulation: no other code can reach the cached results. It’s also reusable for any other function you want to memoize.

Note This wrapper only works for functions taking a single argument. A more sophisticated version lives in Lodash. When functions tend to be called repeatedly with the same arguments, the memoize-one library memoizes only the most recent result, avoiding the memory overhead of caching everything.

5.4 Arguments and function parameters

We often use these terms almost interchangeably, but more formally:

  • A parameter is a variable that we list as part of a function definition.
  • An argument is a value that we pass to the function when we invoke it.

A parameter is specified with the definition, and every kind of function can have them: function declarations (the ninja parameter of skulk), function expressions (the person and action parameters of performAction), and arrow functions (the daimyo parameter).

Arguments, by contrast, are linked to the invocation — values passed in at the time of the call:

  • The string Hattori is passed as an argument to skulk.
  • The string Oda Nobunaga is passed as an argument to rule.
  • The parameter ninja of skulk is passed as an argument to performAction.

Arguments are assigned to parameters in the order specified: first argument to first parameter, second to second, and so on. And if the numbers differ, no error is raised. JavaScript deals with it as follows — if more arguments are supplied than there are parameters, the excess arguments aren’t assigned to parameter names (figure 5.6):

Calling practice("Yoshi", "sword", "shadow sword", "katana") assigns Yoshi, sword and shadow sword to ninja, weapon and technique; katana is excess and isn’t assigned to any parameter. The next chapter shows that even unassigned arguments remain accessible.

Conversely, with more parameters than arguments, the parameters without a matching argument are set to undefined. Calling practice("Yoshi") assigns Yoshi to ninja while weapon and technique become undefined.

5.4.1 Rest parameters

Next we’ll build a function that multiplies its first argument by the largest of the remaining arguments. In old versions of JavaScript that required workarounds (the next chapter looks at them). In ES6 we need no hoops: rest parameters do the job.

Listing 5.9 — Using rest parametersJavaScript
function multiMax(first, ...remainingNumbers) {       // #A
  const sorted = remainingNumbers.sort((a, b) => {
    return b - a;                                // #B
  });
  return first * sorted[0];
}

console.assert(multiMax(3, 1, 2, 3) == 9,       // #C
  "3*3=9 (First arg, by largest.)");
#A Rest parameters are prefixed with …
#B Sort the remaining numbers, descending
#C The function is called just like any other function

Prefixing the last named parameter with an ellipsis (...) turns it into an array — the rest parameters — containing the remaining passed-in arguments. In multiMax(3, 1, 2, 3) the value 3 is assigned to first; because the second parameter is a rest parameter, the remaining arguments (1, 2, 3) go into a new array, remainingNumbers. We then get the biggest number by sorting descending and taking the first element (not the most efficient way to find a maximum, but a nice reuse of the skills gained earlier in the chapter).

Note Only the last function parameter can be a rest parameter. Putting the ellipsis in front of any other parameter brings only sorrow, in the form of SyntaxError: parameter after rest parameter.

5.4.2 Default parameters

When writing an API, one of the greatest privileges you can offer users is sensible defaults. Users love flexibility, but more than that they love when things just work without fiddling with every option.

Consider a case where most ninjas are used to skulking, but not Yagyu, who cares only about sneaking:

Repetitive argumentsJavaScript
function  performAction(ninja, action) {
  return ninja + " " + action;
}

performAction("Fuma", "skulking");
performAction("Yoshi", "skulking");
performAction("Hattori", "skulking");
performAction("Yagyu", "sneaking");

Tedious, isn’t it, to repeat skulking simply because Yagyu is obstinate and refuses to act like a proper ninja? One option is to check whether action is undefined and assign a default:

The manual approachJavaScript
function performAction(ninja, action) {
  action = action === undefined ? "skulking" : action;
  return ninja + " " + action;
}

That’s effectively what default parameter syntax does, more succinctly:

Listing 5.10 — Using default parametersJavaScript
function performAction(ninja, action = "skulking") {    // #A
  return ninja + " " + action;
}

console.assert(performAction("Fuma") === "Fuma skulking",        // #B
  "The default value is used for Fuma");             // #B
console.assert(performAction("Yoshi") === "Yoshi skulking",      // #B
  "The default value is used for Yoshi");            // #B
console.assert(performAction("Hattori") === "Hattori skulking",  // #B
  "The default value is used for Hattori");          // #B
console.assert(performAction("Yagyu", "sneaking") === "Yagyu sneaking",  // #C
  "Yagyu can do whatever he pleases, even sneak!");          // #C
#A The assignment sets a default value for the parameter
#B If the value isn’t passed in, the default value is used
#C The passed value is used

Any values can be assigned to default parameters — primitives such as numbers or strings, but also objects, arrays and even functions. Values are evaluated on each call, from left to right, and later defaults can reference earlier parameters:

Listing 5.11 — Referencing previous parameters from a defaultJavaScript
function performAction(ninja, action = "skulking",
                     message = ninja + " " + action) {   // #A
  return message;
}

assert(performAction("Yoshi") === "Yoshi skulking", "Yoshi is skulking");
#A Arbitrary expressions can be used as default parameter values, even referencing previous function parameters

Even though JavaScript allows this, the authors urge caution: it doesn’t enhance readability and should be avoided where possible. But moderate use of default parameters — to avoid null values, or as simple flags configuring behaviour — can lead to much simpler and more elegant code.

5.5 Declaring functions in TypeScript

So far we’ve been in pure JavaScript, where any function can be called with any number of arguments of any type. To ensure an argument has the expected type we’d need a runtime check:

Listing 5.12 — Checking argument types in JavaScriptJavaScript
const doubleNumber = (x) => {
  if (typeof x !== "number") {       // #A
    throw new Error(`Expected x to be a number, but received `
      + `type ${typeof x}.`);
  }
  return x * 2;
}

doubleNumber("abc");   // #B
#A The typeof operator tells us what type of value is currently stored in the given variable
#B This function call will yield an error because typeof "abc" is "string"

The lack of explicit typing, combined with JavaScript’s tendency to implicitly convert values from one type to another, is one of the most common sources of errors. No matter how much you test, there may be an edge case you hadn’t considered where (for example) a library call returns null when you expected a number, and that null gets passed around until it wreaks havoc.

TypeScript lets you avoid these errors while writing less code — and lets you document functions via a special comment syntax called TSDoc. (For a refresher on using TypeScript, see section 2.1.)

5.5.1 Defining parameter types

In TypeScript you annotate functions to indicate each parameter’s expected type, and the compiler checks each call’s arguments against those requirements.

Listing 5.13 — Defining parameter types in TypeScriptTypeScript
const doubleNumber = (x: number) => x * 2;  // #A

doubleNumber("abc");                          // #B
#A number is a type annotation. It has no effect on the code’s behaviour at runtime.
#B This line will trigger an error when the code is typechecked

When the compiler converts this to JavaScript it simply strips the annotation: there’s no runtime check. That simplicity is a big reason for TypeScript’s success — type guarantees without any cost in code size or performance.

TypeScript also supports rest and default parameters. Here’s the rest parameter example from section 5.4.1, annotated:

Typed rest parametersTypeScript
function multiMax(first: number, ...remainingNumbers: number[]) {
  const sorted = remainingNumbers.sort((a, b) => {
    return b - a;
  });
  return first * sorted[0];
}

The number[] annotation indicates that remainingNumbers is an array of numbers. Defaults are even simpler, because the compiler can infer the parameter type from the default:

Typed default parametersTypeScript
function performAction(ninja: string, action = "skulking") {
  return ninja + " " + action;
}

performAction("Fuma");
performAction("Yoshi", undefined);
performAction("Yagyu", "sneaking");

Here the compiler infers that action should be a string, and the type checker allows all three calls. In the first two the default is used, in the third the argument; either way action is a string, so the implicit type is satisfied.

It’s also possible to declare the type explicitly alongside a default — say to allow multiple types:

Explicit type plus defaultTypeScript
function performAction(ninja: string, action: string | null = "skulking") {
  if (action === null) {
    return ninja + " did nothing";
  }
  return ninja + " " + action;
}

Here string | null means action can be either a string or null. Inferring types is a great convenience, and the checker does it well in many places — including function return values. But just because it can infer a type doesn’t always mean it should.

5.5.2 Defining return types in TypeScript

TypeScript requires types for all function parameters (except those with defaults). Return types are different, because there’s a reasonable way to infer them: look at every type that could be returned and create a union. So code like this “just works”, with no annotations other than the argument:

Listing 5.14 — Implicit function return types in TypeScriptTypeScript
const capitalize = (str: string) =>                 // #A
  str.length === 0 ? "" : str[0].toUpperCase() + str.slice(1); // #B

const city = capitalize("seattle");                   // #C

console.assert(city === "Seattle",
  "Seattle is capitalized");
#A Declares the type of the str argument but not the return type of the function
#B str.slice(1) returns a copy of str without the first character
#C The type of the city variable is inferred to match the return type of capitalize

In VS Code you can hover over capitalize to see the generated type:

const capitalize: (str: string) => string

That indicates a function taking a string argument and returning a string. A return type can also be set explicitly, with an annotation after the argument list:

Explicit return typeTypeScript
const capitalize = (str: string): string =>
  str.length === 0 ? "" : str[0].toUpperCase() + str.slice(1);

Why set a return type you don’t have to? Some developers find it useful for preventing mistakes — with a set of complex conditionals it ensures you don’t leave cases unhandled:

An unhandled caseTypeScript
const numberSign = (num: number): "positive" | "negative" => {
  if (num > 0) {
    return "positive";
  } else if (num < 0) {
    return "negative";
  }
}

Type checking this code gives an error:

numberSign.ts:1:35 - error TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and
return type does not include 'undefined'.

1 const numberSign = (num: number): "positive" | "negative" => {

That’s a good catch: we forgot to handle zero! Here’s the corrected version the type checker accepts:

Handling every caseTypeScript
const numberSign = (num: number): "positive" | "negative" | "zero" => {
  if (num > 0) {
    return "positive";
  } else if (num < 0) {
    return "negative";
  }
  return "zero";
}

This is a pattern in TypeScript more generally: you can get away with declaring very few types, but the more you declare, the more the type checker can help you.

Note If you prefer explicit return types in your projects, the typescript-eslint rule explicit-function-return-type enforces that preference.

5.5.3 Function overloading

Nothing in JavaScript says a function must always take the same kinds of arguments. TypeScript gives you multiple possible types per parameter, but sometimes a single type signature isn’t enough. Say we want a compare function taking either two numbers or two strings; a first pass accepts either a number or a string for each argument:

Listing 5.15 — A function with a single type signature that accepts multiple typesTypeScript
function compare(a: string | number, b: string | number) {
  if (typeof a === "string") {                                // #A
    if (typeof b === "number") {                              // #B
      throw new Error("Cannot compare a string to a number"); // #B
    }                                                         // #B
    return a.localeCompare(b);
  } else {
    if (typeof b === "string") {                              // #C
      throw new Error("Cannot compare a number to a string"); // #C
    }                                                         // #C
    if (a === b) return 0;
    return a < b ? -1 : 1;
  }
}

console.assert(compare("a", "b") < 0, "a is less than b");
console.assert(compare(2, 1) > 0, "2 is greater than 1");
#A Uses a runtime check to determine whether we’re comparing two strings or two numbers
#B Makes another runtime check to ensure that the second argument is a string like the first
#C Makes another runtime check to ensure that the second argument is a number like the first

Clearly this isn’t ideal: lots of extra runtime code just to check the argument types we want. Isn’t there a way to have the type checker verify those calls instead? The answer is function overloading: define the function as before, but preface it with additional type signatures.

Listing 5.16 — A function with overload signaturesTypeScript
function compare(a: string, b: string): number;   // #A
function compare(a: number, b: number): number;   // #A

function compare(a: string | number, b: string | number) { // #B
  if (typeof a === "string") {           // #C
    return a.localeCompare(b as string); // #D
  } else {
    if (a === b) return 0;
    return a < (b as number) ? -1 : 1; // #E
  }
}
#A The overload type signatures for the function
#B The implementation type signature for the function
#C Uses a runtime check to determine whether we’re comparing two strings or two numbers
#D As of TypeScript 5.5, the type checker isn’t smart enough to infer types based on overload signatures, so we use b as string
#E Just as in the string comparison case, we use b as number to assert that the argument types match

The key is that the type checker only allows calls matching one of the overload signatures, so compare("c", 3) or compare(3, "c") fail at type check time. We can therefore be confident the argument types match — using as to convey that to the checker.

Recognise that, like all TypeScript features, overloads only matter to the type checker. That’s very different from overloads in languages like C++, where each signature has a separate implementation. As a philosophical matter, TypeScript never adds code you didn’t write — except when transpiling newer ECMAScript features to older targets.

Note JavaScript engines tend to optimise functions more effectively when they’re consistently called with the same argument types. In practice this only matters for functions called a lot, but it’s worth keeping in mind for performance-critical parts of your application.

One more note: the overload syntax above only works with the function keyword. You can provide overloads for functions of any kind — even arrow functions — by defining a type with those signatures and annotating the function with it:

Listing 5.17 — An arrow function with overload signaturesTypeScript
type CompareFunction = {         // #A
  (a: string, b: string): number; // #A
  (a: number, b: number): number; // #A
}                                // #A

const compare: CompareFunction =                  // #B
  (a: string | number, b: string | number) => { // #B
    if (typeof a === "string") {
      return a.localeCompare(b as string);
    } else {
      if (a === b) return 0;
      return a < (b as number) ? -1 : 1;
    }
}
#A Defines a type called CompareFunction with a list of overload signatures
#B The type annotation indicates that compare is a CompareFunction

5.5.4 Documenting functions with TSDoc

Type annotations provide information the checker can use to catch errors — but that isn’t their only benefit: they’re very useful to humans. Knowing what types a function expects makes it much easier to understand what it does, and in a TypeScript-aware editor like VS Code you can simply hover to see the type information.

There’s also the traditional method of explaining a function: comments. What if we could have the best of both worlds — human-readable comments designed to be used alongside type annotations, so tools and editors provide contextual information? That’s exactly what TSDoc gives us: an official comment format automatically supported by TypeScript-aware tooling.

Listing 5.18 — A function with TSDoc commentsTypeScript
/**                                                           // #A
 * Emits a string describing a ninja performing an action.    // #B
 *
 * @param ninja – The name of a ninja                          // #C
 * @param action – The action the ninja is performing, or `null` if // #C
 *                 they're doing nothing (defaults to "skulking")  // #C
 * @returns A string of the form "Yagyu sneaking"              // #D
 */
function performAction(ninja: string, action: string | null = "skulking") {
  if (action === null) {
    return ninja + " did nothing";
  }
  return ninja + " " + action;
}
#A /** indicates the beginning of a TSDoc comment for the function that follows
#B Freeform text without an @ tag describes the function as a whole
#C Each @param tag describes a function parameter
#D The @returns tag describes the return value
